title: Explaining a diagnosis of DCIS

header.contentArea: Explaining ductal carcinoma in situ and its management
guidelineVersions: NICE NG101 Early and locally advanced breast cancer (updated 2026)

related.why: The screening pathway through which DCIS is commonly detected

brief.setting: Breast clinic, results appointment following screening-detected microcalcification
brief.scenario: Mrs Yilmaz, 49, was recalled after screening microcalcification and has had a core biopsy confirming ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), intermediate grade.
brief.task: Explain this diagnosis and the treatment options. You have 7 minutes.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: DCIS is a cancer diagnosis, but a distinct one from invasive cancer, with a different, generally better prognosis - explain this distinction clearly without minimising or over-alarming.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Either calling it "not really cancer" in a way that later feels misleading, or delivering it exactly like an invasive cancer diagnosis without explaining the important differences.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Your biopsy has confirmed a finding called DCIS - can I explain exactly what that means?"

flow: Explain why it still needs treatment despite being non-invasive

grid.label: Delivering the result
grid.fail: Delivers the result in a way that either omits it's a form of cancer, or delivers it exactly as an invasive cancer diagnosis with no distinction.
grid.pass: States clearly that the biopsy shows DCIS, a form of early, non-invasive breast cancer.
grid.high: Pauses briefly after using the word "cancer" to let this land, recognising the word itself carries weight regardless of the important distinctions to follow.

grid.label: Explaining what DCIS is
grid.fail: Cannot explain what makes DCIS different from invasive cancer.
grid.pass: Explains that DCIS means abnormal cells are confined within the milk ducts and have not spread into surrounding breast tissue, unlike invasive cancer.
grid.high: Explains that this is why DCIS cannot spread elsewhere in the body while it remains in this form, which is an important reassurance, without saying it therefore doesn't matter.

grid.label: Explaining why treatment is still needed
grid.fail: Cannot explain why DCIS needs treatment if it hasn't spread.
grid.pass: Explains that DCIS is treated to prevent it progressing to invasive cancer over time, which it can do if left untreated.
grid.high: Explains that grade (as in her case, intermediate) helps estimate this risk, without overstating certainty about an individual's specific risk.

grid.label: Explaining treatment options
grid.fail: Presents only one treatment option as though it were the only choice.
grid.pass: Explains that treatment usually involves surgery (breast-conserving surgery or mastectomy depending on extent), often with radiotherapy after breast-conserving surgery.
grid.high: Explains that axillary surgery (e.g. sentinel node biopsy) isn't routinely needed for pure DCIS, distinguishing this from invasive cancer management.

grid.label: Addressing concerns
grid.fail: Dismisses her confusion about whether this is "really" cancer.
grid.pass: Responds patiently and honestly to her confusion about the nature of the diagnosis.
grid.high: Validates that this distinction is genuinely confusing for many patients, without making her feel she should have understood it immediately.

grid.label: Next steps and closing
grid.fail: Ends without a clear next step or referral.
grid.pass: Confirms referral to the breast MDT/surgical team to plan treatment and arranges a further discussion of specifics.
grid.high: Checks how she's feeling about everything before closing, recognising a cancer diagnosis, even a favourable one, is still significant news.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Good news really, it's not proper cancer, it's just DCIS, you'll just need a small operation.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Not really, no, don't worry about it.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Right, that's everything - you can head back to the waiting room now.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Your biopsy has confirmed a finding called DCIS - can I explain exactly what that means?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: Please do, the letter mentioned cancer and I've been so worried.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: DCIS stands for ductal carcinoma in situ - it means there are abnormal cells confined within the milk ducts, which haven't spread into the surrounding breast tissue, unlike invasive cancer.

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: So why do I need treatment if it hasn't spread?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Because if left untreated, DCIS can develop into invasive cancer over time, so treatment now aims to prevent that.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Treatment usually involves surgery - either removing the affected area with breast-conserving surgery, often followed by radiotherapy, or mastectomy if the area is more extensive.

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: I'm confused whether I actually have cancer or not.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: That confusion makes complete sense - it is a form of cancer, but a very early, non-invasive one, which is an important distinction for how it behaves and how we treat it.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'll refer you to our surgical team to discuss the specific treatment plan for you.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Your biopsy has confirmed a diagnosis called DCIS - I want to take a moment to properly explain what that means, since it's a form of cancer, but a quite specific and different one.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: [Pauses.] Okay - I did see the word cancer in the letter and it's been on my mind constantly.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That's completely understandable. DCIS means abnormal cells are present, but they're confined within the milk ducts and haven't broken through into the surrounding breast tissue - which is what makes invasive cancer able to spread elsewhere in the body. While it stays in this form, it can't do that.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: Then why treat it at all?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Because DCIS can progress into invasive cancer over time if left untreated, and the grade found on your biopsy - intermediate, in your case - helps give a sense of that risk, though it's not possible to predict this with certainty for any individual.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Treatment is usually surgical - either removing the affected area with breast-conserving surgery, often with radiotherapy afterward, or mastectomy if it's more widespread. Because it's non-invasive, axillary surgery like sentinel node biopsy isn't usually needed, unlike with invasive cancer.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: I still don't fully understand if I actually have 'cancer' cancer.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Honestly, this is one of the most confusing distinctions in breast medicine, and it's completely reasonable to find it hard to hold both things at once - yes, it's technically cancer, and yes, it behaves very differently from the invasive cancer people usually picture when they hear that word.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'll refer you to our surgical team to plan the specifics with you. Before we finish, how are you feeling, taking all of this in?

failures.move: Describing DCIS as "not really cancer" without explaining the actual distinction (confined to ducts, non-invasive).
failures.consequence: Can feel misleading later if the patient later learns it is classified as a cancer, undermining trust in how the diagnosis was communicated.

failures.move: Failing to explain why treatment is needed if the condition hasn't spread.
failures.consequence: Leaves the patient's most natural question unanswered, risking confusion about or reluctance toward treatment.

failures.move: Presenting only one treatment option as if it were the only choice.
failures.consequence: Removes the patient's ability to weigh breast-conserving surgery against mastectomy as genuine options depending on extent of disease.

recovery.when: You said this wasn't really cancer
recovery.line: I should be more precise - this is a form of cancer, but a distinct, non-invasive one, and that distinction matters.

recovery.when: You didn't explain why treatment is needed
recovery.line: Let me explain why we still treat this, even though it hasn't spread.

knowledge.fact: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) refers to abnormal cells confined within the breast ducts, without invasion into surrounding breast tissue, distinguishing it from invasive breast cancer.
Untreated DCIS can progress to invasive breast cancer over time; the grade of DCIS found on biopsy helps estimate, though not precisely predict, this risk.

Treatment for DCIS is generally surgical (breast-conserving surgery, often with radiotherapy, or mastectomy for more extensive disease); axillary staging surgery is not routinely required for pure DCIS.

recall.think: DCIS is cancer, but non-invasive; explain why treatment matters; offer real options.
recall.say: "Yes, it's technically cancer, and it behaves very differently from invasive cancer."
do: DCIS cells are confined to the ducts
Present surgery options: BCS or mastectomy

numbers.meaning: of screen-detected breast cancers are DCIS
estimated risk of progression to invasive cancer if untreated, varying by grade

recall.trap: Calling it "not really cancer" or skipping why treatment matters
recall.finish: Clear DCIS understanding, real options, referral arranged.

partner.actorBrief: You are Mrs Yilmaz, 49, recalled after screening, with a core biopsy confirming intermediate-grade DCIS. You saw the word 'cancer' in your results letter and have been very anxious, and you're confused about whether you actually 'have cancer'.

reveals.trigger: Candidate delivers the result carefully, acknowledging the word cancer
reveals.finding: You reveal you've been anxious since seeing that word in your letter.

reveals.trigger: Candidate explains the distinction between DCIS and invasive cancer clearly
reveals.finding: You understand better but remain confused about the terminology.

reveals.trigger: Candidate patiently addresses your confusion about whether this 'counts' as cancer
reveals.finding: You feel more settled, even if the distinction still feels odd to you.

push.question: Do I actually have cancer or not?
push.expect: Give an honest, patient answer: yes, it is a form of cancer, but a distinct, non-invasive one, without contradicting this later.

push.question: Why do I need surgery if it hasn't spread anywhere?
push.expect: Explain that DCIS can progress to invasive cancer over time if untreated, which is why treatment is still recommended.

curveballs.prompt: A friend told me DCIS is basically nothing to worry about - is that true?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Gently correct this oversimplification, explaining that while DCIS has a better prognosis than invasive cancer, it is still a diagnosis that needs proper treatment and follow-up.

curveballs.prompt: Could this have already turned into something worse without me knowing?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Reassure her that the biopsy specifically assessed for this, and if there had been invasive elements, the report would have said so, without offering false absolute certainty.
